items.title: 4.6 Elementary Row Operations on a Matrix

blocks.text: Usually, a given system of linear equations is reduced to a simple equivalent system by applying elementary operations which are stated as below:

items: (ii) Multiplying an equation by a non-zero number.
(iii) Adding a multiple of one equation to another equation.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why are these three operations allowed? None of them changes the solutions of the system.
Take \(x + y = 3\) and \(x - y = 1\), whose solution is \(x = 2\), \(y = 1\).
(i) Writing the two equations in the other order changes nothing.
(ii) Multiplying \(x - y = 1\) by 2 gives \(2x - 2y = 2\): the same pairs \((x, y)\) satisfy it.
(iii) Adding the first equation to the second gives \(2x = 4\): \(x = 2\), \(y = 1\) still fits, and now \(y\) has been removed.
Operation (iii) is the one that eliminates a variable; (i) and (ii) only tidy the system up.
The number in (ii) must be non-zero: multiplying by 0 would wipe out an equation and lose information.
Corresponding to these three elementary operations, the following elementary row operations are applied to matrices to obtain equivalent matrices.

items: (ii) Multiplying a row by a non-zero number
(iii) Adding a multiple of one row to another row.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Matrices \(A\) and \(B\) are equivalent if \(B\) can be obtained by applying in turn a finite number of row operations on \(A\).
Notations that are used to represent row operations for I to III are given below:

items: Interchanging \(R_i\) and \(R_j\) is expressed as \(R_i \leftrightarrow R_j\).
Adding \(k\) times \(R_j\) to \(R_i\) is expressed as \(R_i + kR_j \to R_i'\)

blocks.text:
(\(R_i'\) is the new row obtained after applying the row operation).
For equivalent matrices \(A\) and \(B\), we write \(A\ \underset{\sim}{R}\ B\).
If \(A\ \underset{\sim}{R}\ B\) then \(B\ \underset{\sim}{R}\ A\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Here \(R_1, R_2, R_3, \ldots\) stand for the first, second, third, ... rows of the matrix. Each row of a matrix plays the part of one equation, so a row operation is exactly an equation operation written in matrix language.
A small illustration with \(A = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\):
\(R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2\) gives
\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\]
\(\frac{1}{2}R_1 \to R_1'\) (on \(A\)) gives
\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\]
\(R_2 + \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)R_1 \to R_2'\) (on \(A\)) gives
\[\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]
In the last one only \(R_2\) changes: \((1, 3) - \frac{1}{2}(2, 4) = (0, 1)\). The row we add (\(R_1\)) itself stays the same.
Why does \(A\ \underset{\sim}{R}\ B\) give \(B\ \underset{\sim}{R}\ A\)? Every row operation can be undone by another row operation: a swap by the same swap, \(kR_i\) by \(\frac{1}{k}R_i\), and \(R_i + kR_j\) by \(R_i - kR_j\).

Upper Triangular Matrix: A square matrix \(A = [a_{ij}]\) is called an upper triangular matrix if all elements below the principal diagonal are zero, that is,
\[a_{ij} = 0 \text{ for all } i > j\]

Lower Triangular Matrix: A square matrix \(A = [a_{ij}]\) is said to be lower triangular matrix if all elements above the principal diagonal are zero, that is,
\[a_{ij} = 0 \text{ for all } i < j\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to read \(i > j\): \(i\) is the row number and \(j\) the column number. The entries with \(i > j\) (row number bigger) are exactly the ones below the principal diagonal. In a \(3 \times 3\) matrix they are \(a_{21}\), \(a_{31}\), \(a_{32}\).
The entries with \(i < j\) are above the diagonal: \(a_{12}\), \(a_{13}\), \(a_{23}\).
The diagonal itself (\(i = j\)) can contain anything, even zeros.

Triangular Matrix: A square matrix \(A\) is named as triangular matrix whether it is upper triangular or lower triangular. For example, the matrices
\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 6\end{bmatrix}\]
and
\[\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 5 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]
are triangular matrices of order 3 and 4 respectively. The first matrix is upper triangular while the second is lower triangular.

blocks.title: Remember!
blocks.text: Diagonal matrices are both upper triangular and lower triangular.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is a diagonal matrix both? In a diagonal matrix every entry off the diagonal is zero, so the entries below the diagonal are zero (upper triangular) and the entries above it are zero too (lower triangular). The same is true of scalar matrices, the unit matrix \(I\) and the square null matrix.
Where this is going: in the next section we use row operations to turn a matrix into echelon form. For a square matrix that form is upper triangular, with zeros below the diagonal, which makes the equations easy to solve from the bottom up.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Three elementary row operations: interchange two rows, multiply a row by a non-zero number, add a multiple of one row to another row.
2. Notation: \(R_i \leftrightarrow R_j\), \(kR_i \to R_i'\), \(R_i + kR_j \to R_i'\).
3. \(A\ \underset{\sim}{R}\ B\) means \(B\) comes from \(A\) by a finite number of row operations; then also \(B\ \underset{\sim}{R}\ A\).
4. Upper triangular: \(a_{ij} = 0\) for \(i > j\) (zeros below the diagonal). Lower triangular: \(a_{ij} = 0\) for \(i < j\) (zeros above it).
5. Triangular matrices are square; diagonal matrices are both upper and lower triangular.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Multiplying a row by 0. This is not an elementary row operation; the multiplier must be non-zero.
2. In \(R_i + kR_j \to R_i'\), changing \(R_j\) as well. Only \(R_i\) changes.
3. Writing "\(=\)" between equivalent matrices. They are not equal; write \(\underset{\sim}{R}\).
4. Mixing up upper and lower: an upper triangular matrix has its zeros in the lower part.
5. Calling a non-square matrix triangular. Only square matrices are triangular in this definition.
